source.title: Scalable Complexity Control Facilitates Reasoning Ability of LLMs
source.authors: Liangkai Hang; Junjie Yao; Zhiwei Bai; Tianyi Chen; Yang Chen; Rongjie Diao; Hezhou Li; Pengxiao Lin; Zhiwei Wang; Cheng Xu; Zhongwang Zhang; Zhangchen Zhou; Zhiyu Li; Zehao Lin; Kai Chen; Feiyu Xiong; Yaoyu Zhang; Weinan E; Hongkang Yang; Zhi-Qin John Xu

record.tranche_reason: The study measures test loss over model-size and training-data-size sweeps, but uses these sweeps to examine complexity control rather than reproducing the original scaling-law fits.
record.gate_note: Figure 2 reports test-loss scaling sweeps and is recorded below. Benchmark and SFT results compare capabilities across complexity settings, but do not test downstream predictability with scale or pretraining loss; they are not rows for those versions. Parameter-norm and embedding/attention analyses do not measure the claimed loss or compute-optimal allocation.
record.test_reason: Figure 2 reports test loss across data sizes (0.2B–1.4B tokens) and model sizes (50M–0.8B) under different initialization and weight-decay settings. The authors say γ-initialization gives steeper scaling slopes and that σ-initialization plateaus, so the shape of the loss-scaling curve depends on a training-setup choice (V7). There are no fitted power laws or numbers. The ranges span at most about 1.2 orders of magnitude, so V1's power-law form cannot be checked.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say complexity control (constant initialization rate γ plus larger weight decay) makes test loss descend faster with model and data size than a fixed σ=0.02 initialization. They also report higher benchmark scores. Caveat: Table 1 gains are for SFT models; for base models, Table 4 shows no significant advantage at 0.9B, only at 2.4B.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares complexity-control configurations in model- and data-size sweeps; it does not reproduce the original studies’ power-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test-loss scaling behavior differs by initialization/complexity configuration; the σ-initialized model-size curve is described as plateauing, while γ-initialized models retain lower loss at larger scales.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower-complexity settings (larger γ and λ) raise benchmark scores at a fixed scale, e.g. GSM8K +19.4 for 0.9B SFT models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization rate and weight decay shift downstream capability at fixed model and data size.

record.problems: Figure 2 is the only reported source for the loss-sweep values; the text gives qualitative descriptions but no numerical loss values, uncertainty estimates, or fitted exponents. The tested size ranges are limited relative to the claim's several-orders-of-magnitude scope.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant test-loss sweep results were identified. Benchmark tables and SFT comparisons were left out because they do not measure the power-law loss, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream predictability versions.

untested.parts: Power-law form is never fitted. Ranges are about 0.85 orders of magnitude in data and 1.2 in parameters. The model sweep is data-bottlenecked. Compute is not varied.
Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
Benchmarks compare complexity settings, not predictability with scale or loss. The 0.9B and 2.4B models differ in data, so they are not a scaling series.
No fitted exponents, fitting-method comparison, parameter counting, or compute-optimal split. The learning rate is not reported as retuned per configuration.

record.verdict_notes: No V1 verdict is given. The rows give no numbers or fits and cover at most about 1.2 orders of magnitude. The σ plateau occurs at 1B fixed tokens, a data-bottleneck regime that V1 excludes, so the reader's V1 limits_scope is withdrawn. The leftward shift in r1 reflects efficiency, not slope. Not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fit or report power-law exponents, test scaling over several orders of magnitude, or vary training compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of larger runs.
No fixed-compute-budget search or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is reported.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architectures at a fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regime, or power-law analysis of fine-tuning or transfer is reported.
Downstream benchmarks are compared across complexity settings, not shown to improve predictably with scale or pretraining loss.

The study varies initialization/complexity configurations and reports a plateau for one configuration, but does not compare fitting methods, report fitted exponents, examine parameter-counting choices, or test compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: 0.8B-parameter models, small-complexity configuration
rows.operation_detail: Measured test loss across training-data scales.
rows.note: The text says this curve is shifted left relative to the large-complexity curve, indicating better sample efficiency. Numerical losses and a power-law fit are not reported.
rows.check: The text describes only a leftward shift (sample efficiency) of the small-complexity curve against the large-complexity one. A shift is not a change in exponent, and no values or fits are given. V1 cannot be read from it: the range is under one order of magnitude and there is no fit.

rows.subject: 0.8B-parameter models, large-complexity configuration
rows.operation_detail: Measured test loss across training-data scales.
rows.note: The text says loss is comparable to the standard configuration at smaller data scales, then becomes progressively lower as data size increases. Numerical losses and a power-law fit are not reported.
rows.check: The text says this configuration's loss falls progressively below the σ default as data grows, with 'steeper scaling slopes'. That is qualitative and figure-only. V1 link removed: no fit, and the range is 0.2B–1.4B tokens.

rows.subject: 0.8B-parameter models, standard σ-initialization configuration
rows.operation_detail: Measured test loss across training-data scales.
rows.note: The text says the large-complexity configuration is comparable at smaller data scales and increasingly outperforms this configuration as data size grows. Numerical losses and a power-law fit are not reported.
rows.check: Comparator to r2: a shallower data-scaling slope than γ=0.5 under the same λ. Figure-only. V1 link removed.

rows.subject: Models in the γ-initialization model-size sweep
rows.operation_detail: Measured test loss across model parameter counts.

conditions.value: γ-initialized models; Figure 2 line colors identify configurations

rows.note: The text says γ-initialized models retain a performance advantage at larger scales relative to σ-initialization. The prose does not give separate numerical values for each γ configuration.
rows.check: Loss keeps falling with model size for γ-initialized models while σ-init plateaus. Training data is fixed at 1B tokens for up to 0.8B parameters, so data is likely the bottleneck. V1 excludes that regime, so the V1 link is removed. Per-γ curves are not separated in the text.

rows.subject: Models in the σ-initialization model-size sweep
rows.operation_detail: Measured test loss across model parameter counts.
rows.note: The text says σ-initialization has lower test loss at smaller model sizes but its performance plateaus as size increases, leaving it with higher loss than γ-initialized models at larger scales.
rows.check: The σ=0.02 plateau with model size is at fixed 1B tokens, a data-bottleneck regime, so it cannot challenge V1. It shows that the shape of the size-scaling curve depends on the initialization parameterization. Figure-only.

relationships.condition: Figure 2 sweeps: γ-initialization (γ=0.5 or 1) vs σ=0.02 default, Llama-architecture models of 50M–0.8B parameters
relationships.reason: The authors report steeper data-scaling slopes for γ=0.5 than for σ=0.02 (r2, r3), and a size-scaling plateau for σ-init but not γ-init (r4, r5). Curve shape therefore depends on the initialization choice. Evidence is qualitative and figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Initialization with γ=0.5 yielded steeper data-scaling slopes than σ=0.02, while the model-size plateau observed with σ initialization disappeared with γ initialization.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Loss trends with scale are reported, but the study provides no fitted power laws and covers only the stated ranges; the σ-initialization model-size curve is also described as plateauing (r1–r5).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The reported loss trends depend on initialization configuration, and the σ-initialized model-size sweep is described as plateauing while γ-initialized models retain an advantage at larger sizes (r1–r5).
